title: Українська 101
subtitle: A self-study course in Ukrainian for complete beginners

product.title: Ukrainian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Ukrainian: a stressed, English-friendly pronunciation guide printed right above every Cyrillic word, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Ukrainian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of the Ukrainian Cyrillic alphabet — with the four letters Russian doesn't have — spelling rules that are almost one letter, one sound, a summary of the seven cases including the calling form (кличний), A1 verb tables, and a glossary. Written for English speakers, and at every point where the two are easily confused it also shows how Ukrainian differs from Russian.

blocks.text: Ukrainian is almost always introduced by comparison: "it's like Russian". That comparison is half true and completely useless. Half true because the two really are related — about six in ten basic words are cognates, and someone who already speaks one starts the other from further ahead. Useless because if you're starting from zero, like most readers of this course, the comparison doesn't help you say a single sentence. What you need isn't a map of similarities but a way in.

And the way in is much friendlier than people expect. The alphabet has thirty-three letters, one letter for one sound, and — this is the most pleasant part — **Ukrainian is written almost exactly the way it's pronounced**. The letter **о** is always read *o*, stressed or not. Compare Russian, where *молоко* (milk) is written with three **о**s but pronounced *ma-la-KO*. In Ukrainian *молоко* is read *mo-lo-KO*, just as written. For an English speaker, used to *though*, *through*, and *tough*, that's a gift that rarely gets mentioned.

The genuinely hard part is elsewhere, and this course won't pretend otherwise. Ukrainian changes **the endings of its nouns** according to the word's role in the sentence. In English, "Kyiv" stays "Kyiv" whether it's the subject, a destination, or a location: *Kyiv is big*, *I'm going to Kyiv*, *I'm in Kyiv*. In Ukrainian all three sound different: Київ, до Києва, у Києві. This system is called case, and it — not the alphabet — is what makes most beginners give up.

Ukrainian has **seven** cases, one more than Russian. The extra one is the calling form (кличний відмінок), and it's the one you'll use soonest: the moment you call someone by name, the ending changes. Оксана becomes **Оксано**, Іван becomes **Іване**, мама becomes **мамо**. Addressing someone with the dictionary form — "Оксана!" — sounds like reading a roll call, not greeting a friend. This course introduces it in the very first unit instead of saving it for the back pages.

The good news: at A1 you don't need the whole system. You need the seven cases in the singular, mostly in their commonest patterns, and about three hundred words. With that you can order food, ask for directions, talk about your family, and say what you did yesterday. That's what the twenty units ahead of you promise — no more, and no less.

One more thing about that comparison. Since many learners have brushed against Russian first — through songs, films, or classes — this course occasionally points out the differences directly, marked with ⚠️. That isn't a Russian lesson; it's a fence, so that words that look the same aren't pronounced with the wrong sounds. If you've never touched Russian at all, you can skip those notes without missing anything.

The method is simple and stays the same from unit to unit: one short dialogue you might really hear, a stressed pronunciation guide above every word, a word-for-word translation that shows the original structure, notes on the tricky spots, as much grammar as needed, vocabulary, four exercises, and an answer key. No page is just decoration.

blocks.title: What to know before page one
items: **This course uses standard Ukrainian (літературна мова)** as used in schools, the news, and official documents — the same language you'll meet in Kyiv, Lviv, and Odesa.
**Spelling follows Український правопис 2019** (the 2019 orthography), including forms like *проєкт* and *авдиторія* that it revived.
**City names come from Ukrainian, not Russian**: Київ (Kyiv), Львів (Lviv), Харків (Kharkiv), Одеса (Odesa) — with one *s*.
**The pronunciation guide is printed in Latin letters, spelled for English speakers**, with the stressed syllable in CAPITALS. It's a temporary aid; from Unit 10 on, try covering it with your finger.

blocks.text: This course has twenty units. Each one is designed for a single sitting — about twenty to thirty minutes — and contains one dialogue, notes on that dialogue, one to three grammar boxes, vocabulary, four exercises, and an answer key. One unit a day and you'll finish in three weeks. Three units a week, in seven weeks. Both are fine; what isn't fine is doing five units in one day and then stopping for a month.
Working through a unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, only the Cyrillic and the pronunciation line.** Don't look at the translation. The goal isn't understanding but getting your eyes and mouth used to it. Read it out loud.

**Read it again with the translation and the literal line.** The literal line is the heart of this course. It shows that *У мене є брат* really says "at me there is a brother", not "I have a brother".
**Read the notes.** That's where the tricky spots mentioned in the foreword are.

**Do the exercises without looking back.** Write by hand if you can; writing Cyrillic by hand forces your brain to take the letters apart one by one — and a hand that has written **и** stops mixing it up with **і**.
**Check against the key, then read the dialogue one more time.** The same dialogue will feel different after the exercises.

blocks.title: Three ground rules
items: **Don't skip the next two pages on the alphabet.** Ukrainian gives you a gift few languages do — it's written as it sounds — but the gift only works if you know the sound of every letter from the start. Planting the wrong **г** and **и** on day one will haunt you until Unit 20.
**Don't memorize the case tables at the back yet.** Those pages are for *checking*, not *learning*. Cases come in through sentences, not tables.
**Say everything out loud.** Ukrainian has sounds English doesn't (soft consonants, **щ**, a rolled **р**). None of them can be mastered with your eyes.

front.title: Ukrainian Cyrillic: thirty-three letters, four of them its own

blocks.text: Some Cyrillic letters you already know, because they look like Latin letters and sound the same: **А, К, М, О, Т**. Others look the same but sound different — this is the group that trips people up most, because your eyes read faster than your brain can correct. The rest are completely new shapes, and those are actually the quickest to learn: because they're unfamiliar, there's no old habit to fight. How the pronunciation guide spells sounds: **a** as in *father*, **e** as in *bed* (**eh** at the end of a syllable), **ee** as in *see*, **i** as in *sit*, **o** a pure *o* (no "w" glide at the end), **oo** as in *food*, **ai** as in *eye*, **h** a soft, voiced *h*, **g** always hard as in *go*, **kh** as in Scottish *loch*, **zh** as in *measure*, **'** a softened consonant.

blocks.title: The apostrophe: one mark, one job
items: The mark **'** (апостроф) isn't a letter and makes no sound. It has one job: to signal that the consonant before it does **not** soften, and that я/ю/є/ї after it are read in full, as two sounds.
*сім'я* is read *seem-YA* (family) — not *SEE-mya*. *п'ять* is read *pyat'* (five). *ім'я* is read *eem-YA* (name).
⚠️ Leaving out the apostrophe makes the word unreadable to a Ukrainian, like writing "cant" for "can't" — only worse. Get used to writing it from now on.

blocks.text: Thirty-three letters in alphabetical order. This is the order dictionaries use, so it's worth memorizing — but not today.

blocks.title: Four pairs that get mixed up most
items: **И and І.** *И* sounds like *i* in *sit* (mouth more open, tongue further back); *І* sounds like *ee* in *see*. The difference is real: *ми* (we) vs *мі* — and *син* (son) vs *сін* (not a word).
**Г and Х.** Both come from the throat, but **г** is voiced and soft (*ahead*), **х** is rough and voiceless (*loch*). *гора* (mountain) ≠ *хора*.
**Ц and Ч.** *Ц* is a tight *ts* in one go — the sound at the end of *cats*. *Ч* is *ch* as in *church*.
**Ш and Щ.** *Ш* is one hissing sound; *Щ* is two in a row, *sh* straight into *ch*, as in *fresh cheese*. *що* (what) is read *shcho*, two tongue movements.

blocks.title: Letters that aren't here — and why it matters
items: Ukrainian **doesn't have** the letters **ы**, **э**, **ё**, and **ъ** found in Russian. If you see them, you're reading another language.
Instead, Ukrainian has **і**, **ї**, **є**, and **ґ**. Four in, four out — both alphabets have thirty-three letters, but not the same ones.

front.title: Stress, and good news about spelling

blocks.text: There's one thing that makes Ukrainian much friendlier for beginners than Russian, and usually nobody tells you: **Ukrainian vowels don't change their sound when they're unstressed.**

In Russian, an unstressed **о** turns into *a*: *молоко* is written with three o's but read *ma-la-KO*. Beginners have to learn two systems at once — how to write and how to read. In Ukrainian, *молоко* is read *mo-lo-KO*. What's written is what's said. For English speakers, who spend years learning that spelling and sound part ways, that means half the pronunciation burden disappears on page one.
So what does stress do?

Stress still matters, but its job is narrower: it decides which syllable is said **longer and louder** — it doesn't change the vowel sound. Putting the stress in the wrong place won't make your word unrecognizable; it'll make your sentence sound read off a page. That's why this course prints the stress above every word right up to the last unit.

blocks.text: Three small adjustments that remain
The spelling is honest, but it still has a few habits. These three are enough for A1, and all three will come naturally through the dialogues.

items: **В at the end of a word or before a consonant sounds like *w*.** *Він був* (he was) sounds like *veen boow*, not *veen boov*. That's not a mispronunciation; that's simply how it sounds.

**Voiced consonants stay voiced to the end of the word.** *Хліб* (bread) is read *khleeb* with a clear **b** — not *khleep*. Russian does the opposite, and it's one of the quickest giveaways of an accent. (English speakers have an advantage here: you already say *dog*, not *dock*.)

**The soft sign ь softens the consonant before it.** *Сіль* (salt) isn't *seel* but *seel'* — the tongue presses more broadly against the roof of the mouth, like a very short *y* glide after the *l*. Practice with the pair *дан* / *дань*.

blocks.title: Your first ten words, right now
items: **Привіт** — *pri-VEET* — hi (casual)
**Добрий день** — *DOB-riy den'* — good afternoon (formal, safe with anyone)
**Так / Ні** — *tak / nee* — yes / no
**Дякую** — *DYA-koo-yoo* — thank you
**Будь ласка** — *bood' LAS-ka* — please / here you go / you're welcome
**Вибачте** — *VI-bach-teh* — sorry, excuse me
**Я не розумію** — *ya neh ro-zoo-MEE-yoo* — I don't understand
**Як справи?** — *yak SPRA-vi* — how are you?
**Скільки коштує?** — *SKEEL'-ki KOSH-too-yeh* — how much is it?
**До побачення** — *do po-BA-chen-nya* — goodbye

blocks.text: If you stop reading here and just memorize these ten words, you can already survive half a day in Kyiv. The next pages turn that half day into a week.

back.title: The seven cases on two pages

blocks.text: These pages are for **checking**, not memorizing. If you've worked through the twenty units, every form below has already gone by inside a sentence — and that's how it really sinks in. All these pages do is rearrange what you've already met, so you can see the pattern at a glance.

Seven cases sounds like a lot. But at A1 you only deal with the **singular**, and two of them (знахідний for inanimate nouns, and кличний for neuter nouns) are often identical to the dictionary form. That leaves just four that are really new.

blocks.title: Кличний відмінок — the case Russian doesn't have
items: Feminine **-а** → **-о**: мама → **мамо**, Оксана → **Оксано**, сестра → **сестро**.
Feminine **-я** → **-е**: Марія → **Маріє**, Софія → **Софіє**.
Masculine, hard → **-е**: брат → **брате**, Іван → **Іване**, друг → **друже**.
Masculine, soft / ending in -й → **-ю**: Андрій → **Андрію**, учитель → **учителю**, Сергій → **Сергію**.
Polite titles go along with the name: **пане Іване**, **пані Оксано**, **добродію**.
⚠️ Calling someone with the dictionary form ("Оксана!") isn't a grammar mistake, but it sounds like reading a roll call. Every Ukrainian uses the calling form, even with small children and pets.

blocks.text: Prepositions and the cases that follow them

blocks.title: If you can only remember three things
items: **Location takes the Місцевий, direction takes the Знахідний.** *Я в школі* (I'm at school) vs *Я йду в школу* (I'm going to school). The preposition is the same; the ending tells the story.
**Absence always takes the Родовий.** *Немає* is followed by the родовий, no exceptions: *немає часу*, *немає грошей*, *немає проблем*.
**Possession is flipped.** Ukrainian has no everyday verb "to have"; it says *У мене є…* — "at me there is…", with the owner in the родовий.

blocks.text: Every Ukrainian verb leans on one of two patterns. The only difference is one letter in the third-person singular ending: pattern one uses **-е**, pattern two uses **-и**. Know that one form and the rest follow on their own.
Pattern I (-е-): читати — to read
Same pattern: **працювати** (to work), **знати** (to know), **гуляти** (to go for a walk), **писати** (to write: пишу, пишеш…), **жити** (to live: живу, живеш…), **пити** (to drink: п'ю, п'єш…).
Pattern II (-и-): говорити — to speak
Same pattern: **робити** (to do), **любити** (to love), **бачити** (to see), **вчити** (to learn / to teach), **платити** (to pay), **коштувати** (to cost).
Five verbs that go their own way

blocks.title: є — one word, two fates
items: As the linking word "is / am / are", **є is usually dropped** in the present: *Я студент* (I'm a student), not *Я є студент*.
As "there is", **є is kept**: *У мене є брат* (I have a brother), *Тут є кафе?* (is there a café here?).
The past forms, on the other hand, are required and follow gender: *Я був* (male), *Я була* (female), *Ми були* (plural).

blocks.text: Past tense: one ending, three genders
The Ukrainian past tense doesn't care who's speaking — it cares about **gender and number**. Drop **-ти** from the base form and add the ending.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Verbs that know your gender
items: If you're a woman, you say **Я була** and **Я читала** — always, for life, in every past-tense sentence.
If you're a man, **Я був**, **Я читав**.

English has nothing like this, and you can't skip it: every past-tense sentence makes you choose. Practice your own form until it's automatic, because the past tense is what you'll use most when telling a story.

blocks.text: Future tense: Ukrainian has two roads

The two forms mean the same thing. The fused form (**читатиму**) is one of the features of Ukrainian that Russian doesn't have at all; using it now and then immediately shows you've learned Ukrainian, not translated from another language.
Commands and suggestions
Add **будь ласка** after any command and it instantly becomes polite: *Скажіть, будь ласка…* (Could you tell me…). It's the most useful formula in the whole course.
Zero to twenty
Tens, hundreds, and beyond

blocks.title: Numbers change the word that follows them
items: **1** → dictionary form: *одна гривня*, *один рік*.
**2, 3, 4** → ordinary plural: *дві гривні*, *три роки*, *чотири книги*.
**5 and up** → родовий plural: *п'ять гривень*, *п'ять років*, *п'ять книг*.
**21, 31, 41…** go back to the rule for **1**: *двадцять одна гривня*, *тридцять один рік*.
⚠️ It sounds complicated, but in daily life you only need three forms for money: *гривня* (1) — *гривні* (2–4) — *гривень* (5+).

blocks.text: Telling the time

blocks.title: ⚠️ Пів на третю is not half past three
items: *Пів на третю* literally means "half **toward** the third" — that is, 2:30, not 3:30.
This is exactly where English habits mislead you: *half past two* counts from the hour that's gone, Ukrainian counts toward the hour that's coming (like German *halb drei*).
The hour numbers use feminine ordinal forms (перша, друга, третя…), because the word *година* is feminine.

blocks.text: Days of the week
"On (a day)" uses **у/в + знахідний**: *у понеділок*, *у середу*, *у п'ятницю*, *у неділю*.
Months

blocks.title: Ukrainian month names tell you about the weather
items: Unlike almost every other European language, Ukrainian month names don't come from Latin but from nature: **березень** from *береза* (the birch coming into bud), **квітень** from *квіти* (flowers), **листопад** literally "leaf-fall".
That means you can't guess them from English. But you can remember them through their pictures — and that usually lasts longer.
Dates use the родовий: *п'ятого травня* (May 5th), *першого січня* (January 1st).

blocks.text: Personal pronouns in the cases

blocks.title: ти or ви — the choice isn't neutral
items: **Ви** is for people you don't know, older people, lecturers, officials, your boss, and anyone in a formal setting. It's also the plural "you".
**Ти** is for friends, family, people your own age you're close to, and children.
The switch from *ви* to *ти* is usually offered first by the older or more senior person: *Можемо на ти?* (Shall we say *ти*?). Until that offer comes, stay with *ви*.
⚠️ A safe rule of thumb for English speakers: if you'd call someone "Mr", "Ms", or "Dr" in English, use **ви**.

blocks.text: Possessives

**його** and **її** never change — two free words in a system where everything changes. **їхній**, on the other hand, does change, and that's another difference from Russian, which uses the fixed *их*.
Question words

blocks.title: Де and куди must not be mixed up
items: **Де** asks about **location** and is answered with the місцевий: *Де ти? — Я в школі.*
**Куди** asks about **direction** and is answered with the знахідний: *Куди ти? — Я в школу.*
English uses "where" for both ("where are you?" / "where are you going?"), which makes them easy to confuse when translating. In Ukrainian, picking the wrong one makes the sentence sound broken.

blocks.text: Common pointing and linking words
The core words that come up in the twenty units of this course, in English alphabetical order. Enough for A1 conversation; not enough to replace a dictionary, and that isn't the point.

If you've reached this page because you actually worked through all twenty units — not just read them — you now have about three hundred words, seven cases in the singular, two verb patterns, the past tense, and two ways of forming the future. That's a complete A1. With it you can order food, bargain at the market, ask for directions, talk about your family, and tell the story of yesterday.

What you don't have yet is just as clear: **plural** forms in all the cases, verb pairs **недоконаний / доконаний** (aspect), and adjectives in the oblique cases. All three are A2 material, and all three are much easier to learn now — once the basic patterns are planted — than if they'd been forced in from the start.
Three next steps, in order

items: **Go through this course once more, without reading the pronunciation guide.** Cover the Latin line with a sheet of paper. If you can read all twenty dialogues straight from the Cyrillic, the alphabet is truly yours — and that's a foundation you can't buy any other way.
**Move on to the plural.** Take the ten nouns you use most and learn their plurals in the називний and родовий only. Those two cases cover eight out of ten everyday sentences.

**Only then, verb aspect.** *Читати* and *прочитати* both mean "to read", but the second means reading to the end. English expresses this differently, and it takes time; don't touch it until steps one and two are done.

blocks.text: Ways to keep hearing Ukrainian

items: **Ukrainian-language news with subtitles.** Suspilne and Hromadske broadcast in clean, standard pronunciation — and the news has an advantage people rarely mention: you already know the story from other sources, so your ears can focus on the sound.
**Songs.** Modern Ukrainian music is plentiful and lyrics are easy to find. Singing makes your mouth form sounds English doesn't have without it feeling like practice.
**One children's book.** A1 picture books use short sentences and everyday vocabulary — exactly what you have now.

blocks.title: One last piece of advice
items: **Start speaking earlier than you feel ready.** Ukrainians are among the warmest people toward foreigners who try their language, and the bar for "good enough" is much lower than beginners imagine.
**Case mistakes don't stop people understanding you.** *Я йду в школі* is wrong, but everyone gets what you mean. Staying silent for fear of mistakes — that's what gets in the way.

**Use the calling form.** If you remember only one typically Ukrainian thing from this whole course, make it this: greet people with **Оксано**, not *Оксана*. That one letter tells the person you're talking to that you're learning their language seriously.

blocks.text: Успіхів! — *oos-PEE-kheev* — good luck.
